title: Words: classes, vocabulary, figurative language, sound and form

blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: Identify word classes, vocabulary choices, figurative language, sound patterning and word formation, and analyse what each does in its place.

blocks.heading: Word classes
blocks.text: The main word classes do different jobs in a sentence: a noun names (river, council, patience), a verb states an action or a being (floods, seemed), an adjective describes a noun (muddy river), and an adverb says how, when or where something happens, or modifies another word class (badly, tomorrow). Pronouns stand in for nouns already known (I, she, it, they); determiners point a reader to which one is meant (the, this, some). Naming the class matters only as a step towards what the class is doing there.

blocks.heading: Lexis, fields and connotation
blocks.text: Lexis is the vocabulary of a text; a lexical choice is the choice of one word over its near-neighbours, and analysis asks why this word rather than that one. A semantic field is a group of words from one area of meaning, and a text draws on a field to keep an idea in front of the reader. Denotation is what a word means; connotation is what it suggests beyond that. A connotation is analysed only when the specific association and its effect on the reader are named: "the noun ‘leak’ suggests carelessness and neglect, so the reader blames the maintenance, not the rain" does that; "leak has negative connotations" does not.

blocks.heading: Modifiers
blocks.text: A modifier adds detail to a noun or another word: a premodifier comes before it (a dry season), a postmodifier after it (a season without rain). The choice between them changes the pace of the noun: stacked premodifiers slow the reader before the noun arrives, a postmodifier makes them wait for it afterwards. Precise modifiers are what turn a noun the reader has met a thousand times into one they can see.

blocks.heading: Figurative language
blocks.text: Metaphor says one thing is another (the town is a furnace); simile says it is like another, using like or as (the town lies like a furnace); personification gives a non-human thing human actions or feelings (the fog swallows the ridges). Pathetic fallacy is a kind of personification in which weather or landscape is given human feeling, so the setting carries the mood: a sullen sky does the atmosphere’s work before any person speaks.

blocks.heading: Sound and word-building
blocks.text: Phonology in written texts is sound a reader can hear in the mind: alliteration repeats initial consonants, sibilance repeats s sounds, plosives (b, p, t, k) strike sharply, and onomatopoeia imitates a sound. Morphology is how words are built: prefixes and suffixes adjust meaning, compounds join two words, and a coinage invents one, often signalling informality or novelty, as when a blogger complains of being "doxxed" or describes a "staycation" and the reader hears the freshness of the coinage as part of the voice.

blocks.heading: Worked example: words at work
blocks.text: Take this sentence, written for the purpose: "The river shrugged off its chains and came for the lower fields." The concrete nouns "river" and "fields" give the reader things to see, and the personification "shrugged off its chains and came" gives the water intention: the verb "came" is a choice over "rose", and the effect is that the flood reads as a pursuer rather than a measurement. The field of restraint (chains) followed by release (came for) makes the reader brace for consequences, which suits a text warning a village at night.

blocks.heading: Concrete and abstract
blocks.text: Concrete nouns name things the senses can reach (river, bread, needle); abstract nouns name ideas (patience, loss, freedom). A shift from one to the other changes what the reader is given to hold: a paragraph of concrete nouns lets the reader build a picture, and a turn to abstractions asks them to think about what cannot be seen. "The needle, the thread, the hem" is followed by "what remained was patience", and the sentence moves from hand to idea — which is the shift to analyse when it happens.

blocks.heading: Two word-level errors
blocks.text: The first error is stopping at "positive" or "negative": a connotation is analysed only when the specific association and its effect on the reader are named, so replace "negative connotations" with the association itself, danger, warmth, officialdom, and what it makes the reader feel. The second is naming the wrong feature, a simile called a metaphor, an adjective called an adverb. The guard is the same for both: test the example against the definition before the label is written, because a word named with the wrong feature undermines the point built on it.
